subject: botany_2
question_text: How does guttation differ from transpiration?

insider_note: Three contrasts: the form the water takes, the time of day, and whether the plant controls it. Liquid against vapour is the one to write first.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Guttation
steps.margin_note: Form, time, control. Three lines and the contrast is complete.
lines: In guttation, water is lost from the leaves in
the form of liquid WATER DROPLETS.
steps.why: Guttation pushes liquid water out through fixed pores that cannot close, which is why it is both liquid and uncontrolled.
common_mistakes: Saying guttation releases vapour. It releases liquid DROPLETS.
Saying it happens by day. Guttation occurs at NIGHT.
steps.memory_tip: Guttation is drops at night; transpiration is vapour by day.

steps.label: Transpiration
steps.margin_note: Mirror all three points, and say WHY it is controlled.

lines.text: Drops at night against vapour by day

lines: In transpiration, water is lost from the leaves
in the form of WATER VAPOUR.
It is a CONTROLLED process, because the
steps.why: Transpiration goes through stomata, and because a stoma can shut, the plant has control over it in a way it never has over guttation.
common_mistakes: Calling transpiration uncontrolled. The stomata can close, so it IS controlled.
Giving only the form and not the time. All three contrasts carry the mark.
steps.memory_tip: A pore that can shut is a process that can be controlled.
